brief.head: Mind the windows
brief.text: Sunil Gavaskar kept the ball on the ground, Amit Varma recalled from memory, because in gully cricket a broken window meant losing your ball or bat. {090-S05}

brief.head: Hikes in chappals
brief.text: At IIT, Ajay Shah and his friends made hikes harder on purpose: rubber chappals, heavy loads, hiking at night, and finally all three at once. {090-S12}

brief.head: One ball, twenty kids
brief.text: Upper-class children in India tire of each new toy in three days, Ajay Shah said. In his childhood, twenty children shared one tennis ball. {090-S04}

brief.head: The shutter that isn’t
brief.text: Amit Varma’s phone goes click, but there is no shutter. A phone camera’s “pro” mode is no truer, Ajay Shah said: its aperture and exposure dials are just image processing. {090-C11}

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on how limits breed invention
lead.head: Stupid, therefore creative
body: Ajay Shah opened the episode offended. Amit Varma had called him stupid, he complained, and in any decent age that would have meant a duel at fifty paces.
Varma’s defence was that he had called them both stupid. “We are both creative because we are both stupid,” he said. {090-C01}
The brain, he explained, cannot take in all the complexity of the world. So we tell stories that are simpler than reality, never entirely true but useful, and our creativity grows out of that limit.

Shah took the point into his own field. A storyteller’s stories and a scientist’s models are the same thing, he said, quoting the statistician George Box: “All models are wrong, some models are useful.”
The theme, Varma announced, was how constraints can often lead to explosions of creativity. What followed was a run of stories about people who met a hard limit and found another way.
## Limits that made something

Joni Mitchell got polio at nine and her left hand grew much weaker, so she invented about fifty alternative guitar tunings. Frida Kahlo, bedridden after a bus accident, painted self-portraits from her bed with the help of a mirror her parents set up.
Dr Seuss wrote *Green Eggs and Ham* on his publisher’s challenge to use only fifty words. Dick Fosbury could not master the high jump’s straddle, so he invented the flop and won Olympic gold.
Coco Chanel could not afford silk, so she made couture from jersey. Keith Haring drew in chalk in the New York subway because he had to finish before the transit police arrived.
Varma was careful about what he claimed. Polio was no blessing to Mitchell, he said, “because no one should get polio”.
But it was a blessing to music: “It pushed a person, forced a person into going into different directions and doing interesting things.” {090-C02}
Shah found the stories inspiring. “In India we have people who will give you twenty reasons why X can’t be done,” he said.
## Forced or chosen

Shah drew a line between constraints the world forces on you, such as polio, and constraints you choose. Why would anyone play chess blindfold? Because, he said, “it’s like the constraint is what brings it to life.” {090-C03}
Varma widened the idea. A guitar is a constraint, he said, and so is a keyboard; Shah added the 800-word column and the 280-character tweet. The question, Varma said, is how you look at it.
## Enter the grinch
Near the end, Shah volunteered to be “the main grinch”. Millions of people were struck down by polio, he said, and for most it made life worse. We pick the stories of the few who broke out. {090-C10}

His second caution was mathematical. Add constraints to an optimisation problem, and at best you match the unconstrained answer. “If you respect the frame, then it’s inevitable that as you layer on the constraints, it gets worse,” he said. {090-C09}
Varma was not for a moment saying that polio, or constraints, are good, he replied. The point was to be inspired by such stories, and to get past our own.

Earlier, he had noted that the show itself runs within a limit of sixty to ninety minutes. He signed off accordingly: “We will respect the constraints of your time and we will let you go and do amazing things.”

second.label: Children’s books
second.head: Green eggs on a budget
second.deck: Amit Varma on a publisher’s challenge and the children’s book it produced
body: Bennett Cerf, a founder of Random House and Dr Seuss’s publisher, challenged him to write a full book using only fifty words. It could be as long as he liked, Amit Varma explained, but with no more than fifty different words. {090-S06}

Seuss, whose real name was Theodor Geisel, kept a chart of his words, Varma thinks, and pulled it off with *Green Eggs and Ham*. Varma read it aloud: “I do not like green eggs and ham, I do not like them, Sam I am.” {090-R02}
Asked if he liked green eggs and ham, Ajay Shah said he would be willing to try. Varma, who teaches writing, uses the story with students who fear their vocabulary is too small.

quote.text: The idea was you have to write a full book using only fifty words.

third.head: No off side, no problem
body: Sachin Tendulkar’s cover drive, Amit Varma said, was perfection, “geometry come to life”. Then Tendulkar got tennis elbow, and never revealed in public how bad it was.
Varma has heard, through a very close friend of his who is a very close friend of Tendulkar’s, that at one point he could not lift a cup of tea. A Test against Australia in Sydney lay ahead.
Unable to drive through the off side, Tendulkar decided he would do without it. “And he makes a double hundred without driving through the offside even once,” Varma said. {090-S10}

It was not an innovation story like the others, Varma conceded. He also teased Ajay Shah: a good Indian, “for the purpose of this chapter”, is someone who follows cricket, and Shah does not. {090-J07}
third.caption: Tendulkar’s missing off side

p2.title: Five ways out
p2.deck: Every form is a limit and an opening, Amit Varma argued, from the guitar to the high jump {090-C04}

sections.label: First story
sections.head: Fifty ways to tune a guitar
sections.caption: Joni Mitchell’s fifty tunings
body: Joni Mitchell got polio at nine, Amit Varma said, and for a long time her left hand was much weaker. She later said it gave her an inner life and turned her into an artist. {090-S01}
For someone who wanted to make music, that was a serious problem. She was a fine pianist and could have given up the guitar. Instead she came up with about fifty alternative tunings.

Her method was to hear a chord in her head that she could not play in the usual tuning, and to keep retuning the strings until the guitar produced it. David Crosby, an early mentor, said her experiments blew his mind.
## An orchestra in six strings

She called the unusual chords she found “chords of inquiry”, and heard an entire orchestra in six strings, Varma said, with the top three strings like a horn section. She got to know the instrument more intimately than a conventionally trained player.

The result is a sound hard to file: not quite folk, definitely not quite blues, with plenty of jazz. Had she not got polio, Varma said, she might have learned the guitar normally and experimented far less. {090-C02}
~ Mitchell called herself “a painter derailed by circumstance”, though she painted all her own album covers. *Both Sides Now*, Varma noted, is one of Ajay Shah’s favourite songs. {090-J14}

quote.text: It made me have an inner life and it turned me into an artist.
quote.who: Joni Mitchell, as quoted by Amit Varma

sections.label: Second story
sections.head: A mirror over the sickbed
sections.caption: Frida Kahlo’s mirror
body: Frida Kahlo got polio at six, Amit Varma said, which left one leg weaker. At eighteen, on her way to medical school, she was in a wooden bus that collided with a rail car. A railing went through her pelvis and injured her spine. Through her life she faced some thirty-two surgeries. {#surgeries}
Her dream of becoming a doctor was over. Her parents encouraged her painting instead: they rigged up an easel over her bed, and a mirror so she could look at herself. {090-S03}
The self-portraits followed. She painted the plaster corsets that held her spine together and the equipment around her. *The Broken Column*, from 1944, came after a spinal surgery went wrong.
## Time alone
Varma asked whether being forced to spend time with yourself is, in some ways, a blessing. He and Ajay Shah grew up without the internet or mobile phones.

Sara Rai, Munshi Premchand’s granddaughter, described her childhood to him in vivid detail. He wondered whether losing the constraint of having nothing to do has left us going from sensation to sensation. {090-C12}
~ Kahlo still lived a full life, Varma said, including a tumultuous marriage to Diego Rivera. He loved another line of hers: “Feet, what do I need you for when I have wings to fly.” {090-J13}

quote.text: I paint self portraits because I am so often alone, because I am the person I know best.
quote.who: Frida Kahlo, as read by Amit Varma

sections.label: On writing
sections.head: Just the tip of the iceberg
sections.caption: writing within limits
body: Amit Varma’s writing students often worry that their vocabulary is too small. He has two answers. Read a lot, and it will grow. And it is already enough, since no writer needs more words than her readers know. {090-C05}

Agatha Christie, he said, had dysgraphia and perhaps dyslexia. Rather than give up, she developed a clear, concise style and tight, intricate plotting. “Out of that limitation arises a style that is a feature, not a bug,” Varma said. {090-S07}

Ernest Hemingway’s spare style came partly from filing dispatches on deadline. His iceberg idea held that only about an eighth of what is going on needs to be in the story. “It is not only show don’t tell, but it is show enough and no more,” Varma said. {090-C06}
## Cut to fit
Varma used to complain about 800-word column limits, write 1,200 words and then find that what he cut was not needed. “You need that artificial constraint to get it done,” he said. {090-C07}
His students get a final exercise: no adverbs, no adjectives, no word over two syllables. The aim, he said, is to make them look at their sentences carefully.
~ The great Hindi film lyricists, Sahir Ludhianvi, Gulzar and Javed Akhtar, all wrote to meter and music, he said. The constraints brought out the genius in their work.

quote.text: I do not believe, Ajay Shah, that any writer needs a greater vocabulary than her readers.

sections.label: In sport
sections.head: A flop that won gold
sections.caption: the Fosbury flop
body: In sport, Amit Varma said, the rules are the constraints. Limit the fielders in the outfield in a one-day match, or bring in football’s offside rule, and you change the incentives and so the game.

Baseball keeps tinkering with its rules to keep the game balanced, Varma said, the subject of a brilliant book by Stephen Jay Gould. In a sense it is central planning, which works because a game is not unboundedly complex. {090-R08}

At school, Dick Fosbury could not do the straddle, in which you face the bar and cross it one leg at a time. So he tried other things and, like all heretics, was mocked. One headline said “Fosbury flops”, and people likened him to a fish flopping into a boat.
In 1968, he won Olympic gold with the flop, and it became the standard technique. {#fosbury}
## Not from first principles
Fosbury did not reason his way there from aerodynamics, Varma stressed. “He had a constraint. He simply couldn’t do the straddle,” he said. {090-S09}
And the flop spread only once deep foam mattresses replaced sand and shallow padding, which had made landing on your back dangerous. {090-C08}
~ Varma confessed that he had tried the high jump at school, failed and given up. Thinking of Fosbury, he now wonders what might have happened had he persevered.

quote.text: The Fosbury flop might have been incentivized by a constraint. But the success of it was incentivized by the removal of a constraint.

sections.label: Mini stories
sections.head: Weak glue, strong idea
sections.caption: the Post-it note
body: Amit Varma ended with a run of mini stories, crediting Vaishnav Vyas and Nomsita MS Haritashya as co-creators of the episode.

Spencer Silver of 3M set out to make the strongest adhesive known to man, and failed. One attempt was a spectacular failure, a really weak adhesive. Using it gave him the idea for the Post-it note. {090-S13}

Post-its are now so common, Varma said, that software shows virtual ones. That is skeuomorphic design: new technology borrows the look of the old, as when a books app looks like a bookshelf or a save button shows a floppy disk. It eases people in, but can outstay its welcome.
## Constraints by choice

Some constraints are chosen. Apple, Varma said, set itself targets for how thin and light the MacBook Air would be that existing technology could not meet, and then built the tools to meet them. {#macbook}
Then he set homework: think about the constraints of the artists, scientists and writers you admire, and about the ones that have stopped you from even attempting something.
~ Ajay Shah, meanwhile, still owes recommendations. He had promised five for this episode; when he tried to defer, Varma threatened to demand ten, and they settled on six for the next. {#promise}

quote.text: But that weak adhesive when he uses it, it gives him an idea.

side.boxText: Amit Varma urged listeners to hear everything Joni Mitchell made, starting with *Blue*, singling out *All I Want*, *Little Green*, *River* and *A Case of You*. He had recommended *Blue* once before, he said, in the episode on inflation targeting. {090-R01}

contQuote.text: I wonder in modern times if the absence of the constraint called nothing to do has made us into creatures who are going from sensation to sensation and not spending enough time with ourselves.

stories.caption: the Digger hack
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah’s IIT story, and a high score built on a fracture
stories.head: Can’t play the game? Rewrite it
body: In Ajay Shah’s student days at IIT, the most important male objective, he said, was a keyboard game called Digger. Amit Varma was appalled. “What kind of male objective is that? Shame on you,” he said. {090-J08}

Digger stored its high scores, encrypted, on a floppy disk, and a student’s bragging rights depended entirely on that number. Then Shah suffered multiple compound fractures of his right arm. He was right-handed, and games were played on the keyboard.

With nothing better to do, he disassembled the game’s compiled binary and read it, hundreds of times. He knew the game intimately, and slowly he found the regions of the file where the floor plan of each level was stored.
He found he could change them, so he wrote an editor to design his own levels. Then he built one in which the monsters died by themselves, and left the machine running all night.
“The world champions at the time had like scores of ten, twenty thousand and I re-emerged from my fractured right arm days with a high score of three hundred thousand,” Shah said. {090-S11}
“At one level this might be called adapting to constraints,” Varma said. “Fancy term. This is cheating.” Shah said it was the only time in his life he had read binary.

~ Varma asked the editor, Nomsita, to leave the whole story in and “let the world see what a shameless man this is”. Then he relented: “At one level I just lost respect for you, but at another level I gained respect for you.”
stories.why: Shut out of the game, Shah went a level up and rewrote its levels. Varma called it cheating. Either way, the constraint sent Shah somewhere he would not otherwise have gone: into the game’s binary.

stories.start: And the inspiring story I tell them is the story of the writer Shivani
stories.end: you're breathing, you're lucky, just stop complaining and get on with it
stories.caption: Shivani at the dinner table
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a Hindi writer who never waited for quiet
stories.head: Serve dinner, then write
body: When Amit Varma’s writing students say they have no time, he tells them about Shivani, a legendary Hindi writer of the mid-twentieth century. Women especially, he said, carry a double load of career, cooking and children.
Shivani’s daughter Mrinal Pande told Varma how her mother worked. Shivani would cook, serve the whole family, and then sit down and write as they ate around her. The family knew not to disturb her.

She did not wait for a vacation, or wake up four hours early for quiet. Varma put her reasoning in her own voice: “Whatever little scraps of time I get within that, I will just sit and write.” {090-S02}
~ Varma has interviewed both of Shivani’s daughters, Mrinal Pande and Ira Pande, and her nephew Pushpesh Pant, who was like a son to her.

quote.text: Everyone is constrained. So at some point you’re alive, you’re breathing, you’re lucky, just stop complaining and get on with it.

stories.postscript: Varma has taught more than 2,800 students in his online writing course. {#students}

stories.start: So my next mini story is about the great designer Coco Chanel.
stories.end: other garments and bring them to the fore. So that's an interesting story.
stories.caption: Coco Chanel’s jersey
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a designer who could not afford silk
stories.head: Couture from the underwear drawer
body: Coco Chanel came from a relatively humble family, Amit Varma said. In the early twentieth century she wanted to be a fashion designer, but could not afford the silks and brocades of high fashion.
So her early experiments used cheaper material such as jersey, which was then used to make men’s underwear. {#jersey} Out of it she made classy women’s garments.
That was not typically done. But it made her clothes cheaper, and so more affordable and accessible. {090-S14}

~ What later became commonplace in fashion, Varma said, began with one person’s constraint. In his telling, her thinking went: “I can’t do high fashion with silks and brocades, but I can do beautiful couture with other garments and bring them to the fore.”
stories.why: Lacking expensive materials did not stop Coco Chanel; it pointed her to a new kind of elegance that more people could afford. What began as one designer’s budget became something common across fashion.

stories.start: My next story is about a young artist called Keith Hering.
stories.end: So this is also a story that I find uh interesting
stories.caption: Keith Haring’s subway chalk
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on art made in a hurry, before the police came
stories.head: Chalk it up to the transit police
body: In the early 1980s, Keith Haring was an art student in New York, Amit Varma said. Rather than sell elitist paintings to galleries, he wanted to paint outdoors.
The subway offered him a surface. When an advertisement expired, it was covered with black canvas. {#canvas} That, Varma said, was the ideal canvas for Haring.

But he had to hurry, to finish before the transit police came, and he needed a material that suited speed. So he used chalk. {090-S15} His style adapted to the pace, the medium, the public setting and the certainty that the work would soon be gone.
~ Out of it came quick motifs, such as his barking dog, that became iconic and were copied by others. Later, famous, he was commissioned to paint grand murals that would last. The style stayed.
stories.why: Having to hurry worked like a design brief. The conditions of fast, unofficial public drawing gave Haring a visual vocabulary that later became iconic, and stayed with him even when the hurry was over.

quiz.q: Polio weakened Joni Mitchell’s left hand. How many alternative guitar tunings did she come up with?
quiz.a: About fifty, retuning the strings until the guitar played the chord in her head.

quiz.q: What did Frida Kahlo’s parents set up over her bed after the bus accident?
quiz.a: An easel to paint on, and a mirror so she could see herself.

quiz.q: What challenge did Bennett Cerf set Dr Seuss, and which book came of it?
quiz.a: A whole book using only fifty words; the result was *Green Eggs and Ham*.

quiz.q: Why, by Amit Varma’s account, did Sunil Gavaskar learn to keep the ball on the ground?
quiz.a: In gully cricket, breaking a window meant losing your ball or bat.

quiz.q: What change let the Fosbury flop spread through the high jump?
quiz.a: Deep foam mattresses replaced sand and shallow padding, making back landings safe.

quiz.q: What Digger score did Ajay Shah reach after rewriting the game’s levels with a broken arm?
quiz.a: A score of three hundred thousand, against the champions’ ten or twenty thousand.
